summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing Fibre Channel, a technology commonly used in storage networks. Network management tools can use them with SNMP to see information about Fibre Channel devices and links.

plainLanguage.summary: Storage systems have special cables and switches. This document defines the dials that let administrators check on them from afar.

questions: what is the fibre channel mib
how to monitor fibre channel with snmp
what is a world wide name
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching Fibre Channel ports, switches and links, built to fit alongside the standard interface tables.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel gear, used in storage networks, had no clean standard way to be managed with SNMP. The earlier options were RFC 2837 and a Fibre Channel Management Integration MIB that did not follow the IETF's rules.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4044 defines the FC-MGMT-MIB module, which holds only Fibre Channel specific information, organized into eleven object groups. It says how each Fibre Channel port uses the generic interface table (ifType 56) and ties into the Entity and Host Resources MIBs.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2837. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that replaces it.

today: RFC 4044 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2005 that obsoletes RFC 2837. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Short Overview of Fibre Channel
sections.content:
The RFC describes the Fibre Channel (FC) as logically a bidirectional point-to-point serial data channel built for high performance. It is a general transport for higher level protocols such as SCSI command sets, HIPPI data framing, IP and IEEE 802.2.

Physically it is a set of communication points called N_Ports, joined either by a switching network called a Fabric or by a point-to-point link. An N_Port attaches to the Fabric through an F_Port on a switch. Nodes on an Arbitrated Loop use NL_Ports, and the switch port serving them is an FL_Port. A switch port linked to another switch port is an E_Port, and a B_Port connects a bridge device to an E_Port.

Many FC components have globally unique names, typically formatted as World Wide Names (WWNs), which are expected to persist across agent and unit resets. Frames carry 24-bit address identifiers for source and destination ports. With a fabric in use, a switch assigns these identifiers dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a network of pipes for moving data between computers and disks. Every pipe end has a name tag that never changes (the WWN) and a street address that the switch hands out.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The MIB introduces a Fibre Channel management instance: a separable managed instance of Fibre Channel functionality. Implementations may group functionality into instances however suits them. One example is a single SNMP agent with several AgentX sub-agents, each running a different instance. To keep several instances apart in one SNMP context, every table is indexed by fcmInstanceIndex, an arbitrary integer.

The module contains eleven object groups. They cover basic instance information (name, description, functions performed, optional pointers to hardware and software), basic switch information (domain-id and whether it is the principal switch), basic port information (port name, node name, port type, classes of service, transmitter and connector types, supported protocols), several kinds of port statistics, port error counters, switch port parameters, the logins of attached Nx_Ports, and information about links.

Port statistics come in two flavours. Some counters can grow fast enough to need Counter64, but some older SNMP systems lack it. The fcmPortLcStatsGroup therefore offers low-capacity Counter32 equivalents of the 64-bit class 2 and class 3 statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is a binder with eleven tabs. Each tab holds one kind of information, like what a port is, how much traffic it carried, and what mistakes it made.

sections.title: Fitting In With Other MIBs
sections.content:
Each Fibre Channel port should have its own row in the ifTable of the Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863). This MIB is the media-specific MIB that supplies the extra Fibre Channel detail, and the port tables here are indexed by the port's ifIndex. The RFC gives the clarifications that RFC 2863 requires of such a document.

  • No sublayers are defined, so an FC interface normally has no other ifTable rows above or below it.
  • Virtual circuits are not dealt with, and ifRcvAddressTable does not apply.
  • The value of ifType is 56.
  • ifInOctets and ifOutOctets count the octets in frames between the Start-of-Frame and End-of-Frame delimiters, excluding the delimiters.
  • ifSpeed is 1,000,000,000 for 1Gbs and 2,000,000,000 for 2Gbs. ifHighSpeed is 1000 and 2000 respectively.
  • ifPhysAddress holds the interface's 24-bit Fibre Channel Address Identifier, or a zero-length string if none is assigned.
  • ifInErrors is the sum of several of this MIB's error counters, such as fcmPortInvalidCRCs and fcmPortLossofSignals.

Two more links are defined. fcmInstancePhysicalIndex points to a row in the Entity MIB, and fcmInstanceSoftwareIndex points to a row in the Host Resources MIB. Each is zero when there is no matching row, and an implementation is not required to support a non-zero value.
sections.plainLanguage: Every network device already has a standard report card for each port. This MIB says how to fill in that report card for Fibre Channel, and adds extra pages for things only Fibre Channel has.

sections.title: The Objects and Their Types
sections.content:
The module is FC-MGMT-MIB, registered as fcMgmtMIB under transmission 56. It starts with textual conventions for Fibre Channel values. FcNameIdOrZero is a WWN, 8 or 16 octets long, or empty when unknown. FcAddressIdOrZero is a 24-bit address identifier. FcDomainIdOrZero ranges from 0 to 239. FcBbCredit (buffer-to-buffer credit) ranges from 0 to 32767. FcDataFieldSize ranges from 128 to 2112. FcClasses is a set of classes of service, and FcUnitFunctions is a set of roles such as hub, switch, bridge, gateway, host and nas.

The tables hold details of the instance, the switch, and each port: administrative and operational type, supported classes, transmitter technology, connector type (for example GBIC or SFP), serial number, and speed. Speeds range from 125Mbs up to 10Gbs, plus auto for auto-negotiation. Further tables cover Fx_Port timeouts and capabilities, inter-switch port settings, the logins of attached Nx_Ports and the links between ends.

The compliance statement makes three groups mandatory: fcmInstanceBasicGroup, fcmPortBasicGroup and fcmPortErrorsGroup. The switch groups are mandatory only for instances that manage switches, and fcmLinkBasicGroup is optional. Write access is not required for the read-write objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB gives names and sensible ranges to every number it tracks, so a port speed or an address always looks the same no matter who built the box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Six objects are read-write: fcmInstanceTextName, fcmInstanceDescr, fcmSwitchDomainId, fcmPortAdminType, fcmPortAdminSpeed and fcmISPortClassFCredit. The RFC warns that changing topology or speed could let an attacker gain performance at the expense of other users, and that setting fcmSwitchDomainId to an invalid value could cause denial of service in some configurations.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. The link objects, such as the WWNs and port numbers at each end of a link, reveal network topology, so even GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled and values possibly encrypted.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms, says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and leaves proper access configuration to the operator.
sections.plainLanguage: The remote controls can change real settings, and the readings show how the network is wired. So only trusted people should be allowed to use them, and the messages should be protected.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned transmission 56 as the OID for fcMgmtMIB, matching the ifType value fibreChannel(56). IANA also set up a registry of Fibre Channel port types in three ranges.

  • A standard range, up to 9,999, for types standardized by INCITS Technical Committee T11, under Expert Review and Specification Required policies. The expert is appointed by the IESG and must get approval from T11 through its chair.
  • A private use range from 10,000 to 99,999, from which IANA will not allocate.
  • Values larger than 99,999 are reserved.

The initial standard assignments run from 1 (unknown) to 12 (F/NL_Port); value 3 is an obsolete value that is not to be re-assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of port kinds with a number for each. Some number ranges are for the official kinds, some are free for private use, and the rest are saved for later.

sections.title: How It Differs From Earlier MIBs
sections.content:
RFC 4044 replaces two earlier efforts. The Fibre Channel Management Integration MIB had several problems, according to the RFC: it was not written in SMIv2, which is mandatory; it assumed it would be the only MIB a Fibre Channel product needed, an idea the IETF abandoned in 1992 as non-scalable; it overlapped only partly with RFC 2837; it did not say how Fibre Channel interfaces use the ifTable; and it used OCTET STRING instead of Counter32 or Counter64 for counters.

The RFC removed objects that are not specific to Fibre Channel, such as sensor, trap-registration and generic event objects. The comparison with RFC 2837 says this MIB is a superset of it, with listed exceptions: the fcFeClass1AccountingGroup group and several fcFxPort objects are obsolete, some credit and buffer-size objects are now per attached Nx_Port, and the module table is mostly contained in the Entity MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The older lists were messy and mixed in things that belonged elsewhere. This one is tidy: it keeps only what is special about Fibre Channel and leaves the rest to other lists.
